overview: Pomo is a living umbrella term for many distinct Indigenous peoples and communities associated with seven related languages in what is now Northern California. It is not the name of one centralized state that ruled from 1500 to 1783. Local nations governed their political, family, ceremonial, economic, and territorial lives. Their homelands stretch across very different coastal, redwood, Russian River, inland valley, and Clear Lake settings. Basketry is an extraordinary shared field of skill, but language, place, government, and custom remain specific. Read the atlas carefully. Its 1500 polygon reaches Mexico and also includes Monterey, Morro Bay, Sacramento, and Redding. From 1530 onward it shrinks dramatically, yet omits documented Southern, Southeastern, Eastern, Central, and coastal Pomo places. Neither drawing is a legal or cultural boundary. The label’s disappearance in 1783 is only a map seam. Direct Russian settlement in Kashaya country began later, in 1812, while missions, land seizure, forced labor, disease, massacres, removals, and United States policies unfolded on different local timelines. Pomo peoples and sovereign tribal nations continue.

periods.title: 1500 to 1530: one label covers an impossible expanse
periods.summary: The exact id begins as a single 192-position polygon stretching from Northern California to about 23 degrees north in Mexico. It contains many distant controls while missing Gualala and Point Arena. That gross overdraw is atlas artwork, not a Pomo conquest or unified state.

periods.title: 1530 to 1600: the atlas redraws a much smaller region
periods.summary: The 1530 snapshot replaces the vast shape with a compact North Coast polygon. It contains some Northern, Central, Kashaya, and Russian River probes but excludes documented Southern, Southeastern, Eastern, and coastal places. The redraw is database correction, not a synchronized migration.

periods.title: 1600 to 1650: a repeated outline cannot freeze society
periods.summary: The exact target remains one polygon with the same visible outline and tested memberships. Communities continued their own seasonal work, exchange, family life, ceremonies, and decisions. Repeated map coordinates provide no evidence that one government or uniform custom persisted unchanged for fifty years.

periods.title: 1650 to 1700: topology changes without a historical event
periods.summary: The later files preserve the same bounding box, area, and sixteen positions, although their decoded coordinate hashes differ because of topology encoding. Precision changes from one to three. These are software properties, not evidence of a new border, dynasty, treaty, or population shift.

periods.title: 1700 to 1715: local histories remain larger than the polygon
periods.summary: The atlas repeats its compact feature while many named Pomo homelands remain outside. Stable artwork cannot substitute for community-specific evidence. Rivers, lakes, oak groves, redwoods, coastlines, marriage ties, gathering places, and trade routes connected people without making one centralized territorial state.

periods.title: 1715 to 1750: the final feature spans several generations
periods.summary: One final snapshot feature is assigned all the way to 1783. That long interval does not document a political reign. Historical reconstruction instead depends on archaeology, Indigenous knowledge, later testimony, language archives, and named local histories, each with its own scale and evidentiary limits.

periods.title: 1750 to 1770: colonial expansion approaches from the south
periods.summary: Spanish maritime and overland expansion increasingly affected California, but neighboring peoples and Pomo communities followed different contact timelines. The reviewed sources do not support a blanket first-contact date for everyone called Pomo. Southern Pomo mission entanglement became much clearer after this interval.

periods.title: 1770 to 1783: the map ends before the best documented invasions
periods.summary: Mission San Francisco de Asis opened in 1776 well south of most Pomo homelands. Mendocino-coast explorers sailed past rocky shores without recorded landings there. The atlas ends in 1783, decades before Fort Ross and major documented Pomo colonial disruption, so no historical fall belongs here.

sections.title: Read the map as artwork, not a deed

items.text: The first exact feature is one polygon with one ring and 192 positions. Its bounding box reaches from about 124 degrees west to 109 degrees west and from 23 to 41 degrees north. A shape that reaches Mexico cannot be a defensible Pomo border.

Fort Bragg, Ukiah, Clear Lake, Sebastopol, Point Reyes, Redding, Sacramento, Monterey, and Morro Bay test inside the 1500 shape. Gualala, Point Arena, Eureka, Yreka, San Francisco, and Medford test outside. The mixture exposes a coarse and internally inconsistent cultural-homeland sketch.

From 1530 onward, the polygon tightens to roughly 124 to 123 degrees west and 39 to 40 degrees north. It includes Fort Bragg, Willits, Potter Valley, Ukiah, Hopland, Cloverdale, Stewarts Point, Lakeport, and Upper Lake, but excludes many other documented Pomo places.

The audit finds six exact features, three decoded geometry hashes, three coordinate hashes, and no duplicate target within a snapshot. The later shape’s bbox and area stay constant while encoding and precision change. A database can change its math without any community moving house.

At the 1715 to 1783 seam the exact id vanishes and every tested ownership stack changes. The next 1815 map still lacks this id. That is a software handoff between labels, not cession, extinction, or the legal boundary of any living tribal nation.

sections.title: Keep peoples, languages, and governments distinct

items.text: The Pomoan family contains seven languages: Central, Eastern, Kashaya, Northeastern, Northern, Southeastern, and Southern Pomo. They are languages, not seven accents of one uniform speech. Each belongs to particular communities and places, while present revitalization follows community authority and priorities.

Early researchers expanded “Pomo” from a local name and a Northern Pomo place-name element into an English umbrella. Barrett mapped many villages and language areas, but his 1908 categories and spellings reflect their time. Modern community names and self-identification deserve priority.

Dry Creek describes Pomo peoples as many independent communities rather than one tribe. Historically, local villages were politically autonomous and connected through kinship, exchange, ceremony, and shared practices. Calling the imported record a state invents a capital and central government that the evidence does not show.

The Bureau of Indian Affairs lists numerous distinct Pomo tribal governments, including Dry Creek, Hopland, Kashia, Pinoleville, Scotts Valley, Sherwood Valley, Big Valley, Habematolel, Manchester, Middletown, Potter Valley, Redwood Valley, and Robinson. An umbrella card must never merge their sovereignty.

The Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria identifies Southern Pomo homelands around Sebastopol and Coast Miwok homelands farther south and west. That precise statement contradicts both the 1500 sprawl and later polygon’s omissions. Living territorial knowledge is not replaced by old map shading.

sections.title: Move through coast, redwoods, valleys, and lake country

items.text: Pomo homelands include Pacific coast, redwood forest, Russian River drainage, interior valleys, oak woodland, marsh, and Clear Lake environments. These settings offered different fish, shellfish, plants, game, stone, fibres, and travel routes. Ecological variety helps explain local difference within the umbrella.

Northern Pomo families used permanent coastal or valley settlements and temporary camps in redwood clearings during seasonal hunting and gathering. Redwood supplied building material and bark fibre for clothing. The record describes planned movement through known homeland, not aimless wandering.

Kashia families moved seasonally within a homeland running from the Gualala River toward the Russian River and inland. Food availability shaped travel among villages and gathering places. This Kashia account belongs to Kashia history; it cannot be pasted onto every Pomo community.

Clear Lake communities used abundant fisheries, tules, obsidian, magnesite, oaks, and other local resources. Lake, marsh, island, and stream places were cultural landscapes, not empty supply cupboards. Access and control belonged to named communities, their neighbors, and carefully maintained relationships.

Northern Pomo oral histories and ethnobotany describe deliberate burning, pruning, gathering, and tending for foods, medicines, and basket plants. Most details were documented much later than 1783, so they illuminate inherited knowledge without automatically dating every technique to the full atlas interval.

sections.title: Gather, process, cook, fish, and share

items.text: Northern Pomo accounts describe acorns as a staple requiring harvest, drying, storage, shelling, pounding, leaching, and cooking. Dry Creek also records soups, cakes, and bread, including bread baked in leaves over coals and stored for later use. “Gathered” food could require a very busy kitchen.

At Big River, Pomo people hunted game, caught fish and shellfish, and gathered seaweed, acorns, and seeds. Communities traded for what local environments did not provide and gathered together in times of abundance. Diet and exchange varied with coast, lake, river, and valley.

Clear Lake fishers built light tule boats and worked one of California’s richest inland fisheries. Obsidian from the volcanic region became tools and exchange material. A boat, tool stone, basket, and fishing ground formed a connected technology rather than separate museum categories.

Archaeology traces increasing exchange, obsidian production, settlement differentiation, and specialists in parts of Pomo country. Those patterns changed over long spans and at local scales. They reveal skilled economic networks without proving a single market authority, currency office, or state-controlled trade route.

Koi communities at Clear Lake controlled valued obsidian and magnesite sources and participated in shell-bead production and distribution. Fisheries supported both sustenance and exchange. These achievements belong to specific Southeastern Pomo history; “Pomo trade” should not erase the people managing each source.

sections.title: Build homes, tools, wealth, and everyday technology

items.text: A Big River account describes a principal village with redwood-bark houses near the river mouth. Coastal building practice fit local materials and weather. Tule, brush, earth, and other materials appear elsewhere, so one photogenic house type cannot serve as architecture for every Pomo-speaking community.

A study of the named Salt Pomo community records family dwellings, a large earth-covered dance house, a smaller sweat house, and granaries for acorns and seeds. It is a valuable local reconstruction from later evidence, not a universal blueprint for all Pomo villages.

Northern Pomo toolmakers used local rock and Clear Lake obsidian, while coastal travel brought access to marine materials. Stone points and scrapers survive more easily than cordage, wood, bark, food, and feathers. Archaeological durability can make the stone toolbox look unfairly lonely.

Clear Lake exchange included shell disks, magnesite beads, obsidian, food, and crafted goods. Beads could carry value and adorn clothing or baskets. Their circulation depended on labor, routes, permissions, and relationships; calling them “money” is useful only when local meanings remain visible.

Baskets served gathering, carrying, storage, cooking, washing, sifting, fishing, ceremony, gifts, cradling, and display. Different forms demanded different structures and carefully prepared materials. Basketry was infrastructure with artistry built in, not decoration added after supposedly more serious technology had finished work.

sections.title: Admire basketry without flattening its makers

items.text: Barrett documented plain, diagonal, lattice, and three-strand twining alongside multiple coiling methods and border finishes. He considered the range exceptional, while noting neighboring Huchnom lattice twining too. The 1908 description records mature traditions, not an exact invention date for each weave.

Dry Creek weavers gather and prepare sedge, willow roots, bulrush, feathers, shells, and seeds. The work starts long before weaving: access, stewardship, harvest timing, cleaning, splitting, sorting, and storage matter. A finished basket quietly contains a great deal of botany.

Feathered gift baskets could carry clamshell disks, abalone pendants, and brilliantly colored feathers. Later museum objects show prestige and beauty, but also colonial collecting. Their labels must preserve maker, community, date, and provenance rather than turning “Pomo” into an anonymous style.

Dry Creek explains that women commonly made many baskets while men traditionally made forms such as fish traps and cradles. Practice differed by community, person, period, and purpose. Gendered knowledge mattered, yet a single division of labor should not be declared timeless everywhere.

Museum research recovers named makers and family histories while showing how tourism and collectors reshaped demand. Pomo artists answered markets with innovation rather than merely repeating old forms. Collections preserve remarkable work, but colonial acquisition and lost attribution remain part of the story.

sections.title: Live in families, villages, and wider networks

items.text: Clear Lake land studies describe separate village communities holding recognizable territories, with rights to places and resources shaped by inheritance, permission, and relationship. This evidence fits a network of local nations. It does not support one Pomo land office issuing title across three counties.

Salt Pomo evidence describes multiple leaders representing lineages, marriage links with neighboring Hill Patwin and Hill Wintun communities, and a principal village with satellites. Leadership, residence, and alliance were local arrangements. Other Pomo communities could organize kinship and authority differently.

Gifford reconstructed households and kin ties in Cigom from a former resident’s memory, including marriages, occupations, leaders, and interhouse relations. The study is unusually detailed and unusually narrow. One Eastern Pomo community cannot become the family chart for seven languages.

The Cigom record names women and men across households and ceremonial roles, revealing social life beyond a male-only chief list. Yet its categories reflect interview questions and early anthropology. Women’s gathering, weaving, caregiving, exchange, ritual work, and authority require attention beyond formal titles.

Later ethnography records dances, games, feasts, healers, societies, gifts, and visiting across communities. Such gatherings joined pleasure, obligation, exchange, and ceremony. They were not identical everywhere, and some accounts exposed knowledge that communities may consider sensitive. Public history should leave boundaries around restricted teachings.

sections.title: Teach children and keep languages audible

items.text: A Smithsonian Pomo transport cradle, accessioned in 1899 but made on an unrecorded date, uses prepared willow rods, a protective hoop, woven lashing, a carrying band, and shell beads. The child sat with legs free rather than being tied to a board. This collected object shows care and engineering, not every cradle ever made.

Accounts of women weavers describe children learning by watching relatives gather, prepare, and manage plants before mastering weaving. Boarding schools later punished language and separated children from family teaching. Pomo education persisted through elders, work, stories, classrooms, and deliberate cultural renewal.

Northern Pomo stories recorded with Annie Lake, Edna Campbell Guerrero, and Angelina Campbell were translated with community speakers decades later. Kashaya and Southern Pomo archives follow their own histories. Documentation preserves voices, but no one archive stands for all seven languages.

The Northern Pomo phrasicon available in 2026 preserves “yaʔ pʰik'ana:m pʰowaʔ ʔanu k'edi na,” translated “our baskets are better than theirs.” It credits speaker ES and supplies word-by-word analysis. Source recordings span 1979 to 2005; this sentence's session date is unpublished. It is not claimed interval speech or shared across all seven Pomoan languages.

Tribal programs now build Southern Pomo classes, dictionaries, digital collections, culturally responsive activities, and student support. Federal curriculum research emphasizes technology and cultural protocol across seven languages. Language work is education, family practice, governance, and future-making, not a museum rescue scene.

sections.title: Treat health, water, waste, and toilets honestly

items.text: Freeland’s later ethnography describes Pomo healers using prayer, song, touch, plant preparations, water, diagnosis, and sustained attendance with patients. It also records training and payment. These accounts are culturally specific and late; they cannot supply one medical system unchanged since 1500.

Northern Pomo ethnobotany records plants used for medicine, food, ceremony, tools, and basketry, together with spiritual meanings and careful preparation. Oral history can preserve deep knowledge while also reflecting later change. Exact plant uses should remain with the named community and source.

One account portrays healers as responsible guardians who stayed with patients and sometimes returned payment when treatment failed. It also records practices and beliefs that should not be mocked or converted into biomedical claims. Respect includes distinguishing cultural testimony from laboratory evidence.

The California State Parks Clear Lake script, consulted in 2026, describes middens containing shells, animal bone, and other discarded remains. Middens reveal food, use, and disposal over time, though colonial disturbance complicates them. They are evidence of refuse, not proof of a standardized sanitation department or household cleaning schedule.

No reviewed source securely describes a standard Pomo latrine, privy, sewer, chamber pot, or toilet routine for 1500 to 1783. People lived near dependable water and managed ordinary waste, but the details remain undocumented. The baskets survived history’s filing cabinet; the bathroom plan did not.

sections.title: Place colonial violence after the map seam and continuity beyond it

items.text: Mendocino-coast accounts say European ships passed offshore beginning in the 1500s, while rocky shores prevented recorded landings there. Graton sources document 1579 and 1595 encounters with Coast Miwok neighbors farther south. Neighboring contact cannot silently become first contact for every Pomo community.

Fort Ross began in 1812 in Kashaya territory, after the atlas endpoint. Russians, Alaska Natives, Kashaya families, and others formed a complex colonial settlement; some Kashaya worked there and some marriages occurred. Agreements and cooperation did not erase unequal labor or imperial occupation.

Missions, ranchos, settlers, disease, coerced labor, and land seizure harmed different Pomo communities on different schedules. Southern Pomo people entered mission systems and later farm labor; Northern Coast communities faced Russian and American incursions. The consequences were devastating without being a single event in 1783.

Mexican and United States violence culminated in massacres, forced removals, stolen land, and sealed treaties. Bloody Island in 1850 killed Clear Lake people, including women and children. Native accounts and modern teaching restore agency and testimony that official stories long minimized or distorted.

Pomo nations continue governing, teaching, making art, restoring language, caring for land and water, and negotiating with public agencies. Big Valley’s agreement with California State Parks includes stewardship and tule boat renewal. Kashia basketry and cultural practice also continue within ancestral territory. Sovereignty is living practice.

ending.text: The atlas stops drawing “Pomo” in 1783, but no Pomo people, language, village, or government fell that year. The most clearly documented colonial invasions and state violence come later: Fort Ross from 1812, mission and rancho labor, United States conquest, massacres, forced removals, unratified treaties, rancherias, termination, and restoration. Those histories affected named communities differently and never turned them into one vanished state. Today many sovereign Pomo tribal nations govern on their own authority, while families and cultural workers teach languages, renew basketry, make tule boats, protect gathering places, recover land, document testimony, and care for Clear Lake, coast, river, and valley homelands. A Big Valley-produced documentary deliberately tells Lake County history through Pomo voices. That is the right ending for this card: the map layer disappears, the imported “state” category is corrected, and living peoples continue speaking for themselves.
